summary: Specifies the file transfer protocol, a user-level protocol for moving files between hosts on the ARPANET, including terminal IMPs. Its main goal is to make transferring files and using remote storage easy. It updates RFC 114 and was replaced by RFC 265.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 172 describes an early File Transfer Protocol for moving files between ARPANET hosts. It defines requests such as retrieving, storing, renaming, and deleting files, but leaves pathname rules to each host's file system.

subtitle: An early ARPANET protocol for transferring and managing files between hosts.

tldr.problem: ARPANET users needed a common way to move files between hosts with different file systems.
tldr.mechanism: FTP sends control transactions and file data over the same connection. The first byte of a control transaction identifies its operation, such as retrieve, store, delete, or rename.
tldr.outcome: RFC 172 updated RFC 114 and was obsoleted by RFC 265; it was also updated by RFC 238.

today: RFC 172 updated RFC 114, was updated by RFC 238, and was obsoleted by RFC 265, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The file transfer protocol (FTP) is a user-level protocol for transferring files between hosts on the ARPA computer network, including terminal IMPs. It uses the data transfer protocol described in RFC 171.

The RFC aims to support file sharing and indirect use of other computers while reducing the effect of differences between host file systems. It defines common file operations but does not establish a standard pathname convention; users follow the serving host's rules.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP gives ARPANET hosts a shared way to request file operations. Each host still uses its own rules for naming files.

sections.title: Control Transactions and Operations
sections.content:
FTP carries both file data and control transactions over the same connection. Data transactions contain file contents. Control transactions describe the operation and the structure of the following data; their first byte is an operation code.

The defined operations include retrieve, store, delete, rename-from, rename-to, list-file-directory, username, password, change-data-type, error, acknowledge, and append. Codes from hexadecimal 5A through FF are reserved for experimental use.
sections.plainLanguage: A control transaction says what should happen, and data transactions carry the file contents. An operation code in the control transaction identifies the request.

sections.title: File Requests and Data Types
sections.content:
A retrieve request transfers a copy from the serving host without changing its file. A store request transfers a copy to that host, replacing a file with the same pathname or creating a new one. Append adds data to an existing file, and rename-from must be followed by rename-to.

A store request includes a 4-byte allocate-size field; zero asks the server to use its default. The change-data-type transaction describes later data. The default is a bit stream with byte size 1, and a host must accept data even when it does not recognize the type description.
sections.plainLanguage: Retrieve copies a file from the server; store sends one to it. FTP also has requests to append, rename, list, and delete files.

sections.title: Transaction Order and Completion
sections.content:
Username and password identifiers are usually sent at the start of a connection and do not require acknowledgments. After a retrieve or directory-list request, the server sends the data and an end-of-file indication.

After a store or append request, the user sends the data and end-of-file indication, and the server acknowledges receipt. Rename and delete requests also require an acknowledgment. Either host may terminate the current request with an error transaction or close the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: For a download, the server sends the file and marks its end. For an upload, the sender marks the end and the server acknowledges receipt.
